items.q: What is the fundamental unit of organization in GCP, and how does it compare to an AWS Account or an Azure Subscription?
items.a: The Project. Nearly every resource, IAM policy, and quota is scoped primarily at the Project level -- it's the closest single analog to an AWS Account, arguably closer than an Azure Subscription is, since Azure additionally has Resource Groups as a meaningful sub-Subscription organizational layer that GCP's Project doesn't have an equivalent of within itself.

items.q: How does GCP's Billing Account relationship to Projects differ structurally from how AWS ties billing to an Account?
items.a: A Billing Account is a separate, standalone construct that can fund multiple Projects simultaneously, and a Project can be relinked to a different Billing Account over its lifetime. AWS ties billing directly to the Account itself -- there's no equivalent of a separate billing entity funding multiple otherwise-independent Accounts in the same lightweight way. This makes GCP's model slightly more flexible for scenarios like a single company Billing Account funding many independent team Projects.

items.q: What is the single most important structural difference between GCP IAM and AWS IAM / Azure RBAC that a multi-cloud engineer must know explicitly?
items.a: GCP IAM permissions are purely additive across the resource hierarchy -- a role granted at the Organization or Folder level applies to every Project and resource beneath it with no mechanism for a more specific, narrower assignment to override or reduce it. AWS IAM has explicit Deny statements that can override an Allow, and Azure RBAC at least has the practical convention of assigning at the narrowest useful scope, but GCP has no 'narrower wins' or 'explicit deny overrides' concept in the same way -- once a broad role is granted high in the hierarchy, it cannot be walked back at a lower level. This makes granting broad roles at the Organization or Folder level in GCP a genuinely higher-risk action than the equivalent in AWS or Azure.

items.q: What is a GCP Service Account and how does its identity model differ from an AWS instance profile or Azure Managed Identity?
items.a: A Service Account is a real, standalone GCP resource with its own email-address-shaped identifier (name@project.iam.gserviceaccount.com) that can be granted roles, impersonated, and referenced independently of any single compute resource. AWS instance profiles and Azure system-assigned Managed Identities are more tightly bound to the lifecycle of the specific resource they're attached to. A GCP Service Account is closer in spirit to an Azure user-assigned Managed Identity -- a standalone identity that can be attached to multiple resources -- except GCP Service Accounts are the default and primary pattern, not a secondary option.

items.q: Why is Cloud Storage described as the closest 1:1 naming match to S3 of any service across the three clouds?
items.a: GCP kept the term 'bucket' itself and the same globally-unique-name constraint that S3 has -- no intermediate Storage Account layer the way Azure requires. Conceptually and terminologically, gs://bucket-name/object-key maps almost directly onto s3://bucket-name/object-key, making this one of the easiest single mental translations across all three clouds' storage services.

items.q: How does a GCP Signed URL get generated, and what is the practical implication for who can generate one?
items.a: A Signed URL is generated using either a service account's private key directly, or via the IAM signBlob permission which lets a caller sign on behalf of a service account without possessing its raw key file -- the latter is the modern, more secure pattern, avoiding key file distribution. The practical implication: whoever's identity generates the signed URL must have appropriate Storage permissions on that object, and using signBlob-based signing (rather than a downloaded key) keeps this consistent with the broader 'avoid long-lived credentials' theme running through every cloud's modern IAM guidance.

items.q: What is the Dataproc equivalent of an EMR transient cluster with auto-terminate, and what command pattern achieves it?
items.a: An ephemeral cluster -- created immediately before a job with gcloud dataproc clusters create, the job submitted against it, then explicitly deleted with gcloud dataproc clusters delete right after. Dataproc Workflow Templates can also encode this entire create-run-delete sequence as a single reusable resource, which is arguably a cleaner abstraction than manually scripting the equivalent sequence of EMR CLI calls.

items.q: How do Dataproc's Secondary Workers compare to EMR's Task nodes, and what is the safety rule that carries over unchanged?
items.a: Secondary Workers are Dataproc's Spot/Preemptible-backed compute-only worker pool, structurally equivalent to EMR Task nodes on Spot Instances. The exact same safety rule applies: Secondary Workers are safe for retriable compute-only work because a reclaimed VM just causes Spark to reschedule the affected tasks, but they should never host anything data-critical or serve as the cluster's primary/master role, mirroring the never-Spot-the-core-or-master guidance from the EMR days.

items.q: What is Application Default Credentials and how does its resolution order compare to AWS/Azure's default credential chains?
items.a: ADC checks, in order: a service account key file path in the GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS environment variable, then the attached Service Account via the Compute Engine/GKE/Cloud Run metadata server when running on GCP, then gcloud CLI login credentials for local development. Conceptually identical in purpose to AWS's default credential chain and Azure's DefaultAzureCredential -- the same code authenticates correctly across local dev and production with zero branching -- just GCP-specific environment variable and metadata server details underneath.

items.q: Why is downloading and embedding a service account JSON key file in a container image specifically discouraged?
items.a: A JSON key file is a long-lived, static credential -- if the container image is ever pushed to a public registry, checked into source control by accident, or the image layer is otherwise exposed, that credential is compromised indefinitely until manually rotated. Attaching a Service Account directly to the compute resource (Compute Engine instance, GKE workload via Workload Identity, Cloud Run service) lets ADC resolve short-lived, auto-rotated credentials via the metadata server instead, with no static secret to leak in the first place -- the same principle behind avoiding hardcoded keys on any cloud.

items.q: Since Dataproc clusters have no built-in idle-shutdown timer like Databricks' autotermination_minutes, what are the two practical ways to avoid a forgotten idle cluster costing money?
items.a: Either build the safety net yourself with a Cloud Scheduler job periodically checking cluster idle status and calling the delete API, or -- the structurally better fix -- avoid the problem entirely by defaulting to ephemeral clusters or Workflow Templates (from Day 4) that create the cluster immediately before the job and delete it immediately after, so there's never a persistent cluster left running to forget about in the first place.

items.q: What does the Dataproc cluster staging bucket do, and why might it be confusing to someone new to the platform?
items.a: When a Dataproc cluster is created without an explicitly specified staging bucket, GCP auto-creates one to hold job dependencies (uploaded scripts, JARs) and cluster logs. It's easy to be confused seeing a bucket you never explicitly created show up in the project's Cloud Storage list -- recognizing this as an auto-managed Dataproc artifact (rather than a security concern or a mistake) is a small but genuine piece of platform-specific knowledge.

items.q: What is the one genuinely different structural detail about Cloud Logging compared to Azure Monitor's Log Analytics?
items.a: Cloud Logging automatically captures logs from most GCP services with no manual routing step required -- there's no Diagnostic Settings equivalent that must be explicitly configured per resource before logs start flowing. This is closer to CloudWatch's automatic-logging-for-many-services behavior than to Azure's explicit-opt-in-per-resource model, and it's worth naming this difference explicitly since 'why is there no data' is specifically an Azure gotcha, not a GCP one.

items.q: How does a GCP Alerting Policy differ structurally from having separate Metric Alerts and Log Alerts like Azure does?
items.a: GCP unifies both under one Alerting Policy resource type -- a single policy's condition can be based on either a Cloud Monitoring metric threshold or a log-based metric derived from Cloud Logging, rather than requiring two conceptually distinct alert resource types the way Azure Monitor separates Metric Alerts from Log Alerts. Functionally the coverage is the same as CloudWatch Alarms and Azure's alert types combined; GCP just expresses it through one unified policy concept instead of two or three separate ones.

items.q: This is the third cloud in this plan with the same 'Grafana workspace needs its own identity' gotcha. What is the general principle underneath all three specific cases?
items.a: Any managed visualization or observability tool that queries a cloud's native monitoring service needs its OWN service-level identity with read permissions on that monitoring data, entirely independent of the identity system controlling human login access to the tool's UI. AWS calls this the workspace IAM role, Azure calls it the workspace's Managed Identity, GCP calls it a Service Account bound to the Grafana service -- three different names for exactly the same architectural requirement, and recognizing the pattern rather than memorizing three unrelated facts is what makes this genuinely transferable knowledge.

items.q: When would VPC Service Controls or Private Google Access be relevant to a GCP Grafana setup?
items.a: When the data Grafana needs to query lives behind a private network boundary -- a self-hosted Prometheus with no public IP, or a Cloud SQL instance configured for private-IP-only access. Public Cloud Monitoring and Cloud Logging APIs are reachable through Google's standard API endpoints without special networking; private network configuration only becomes necessary once a genuinely private resource is in the picture, mirroring the same conditional need for VPC Endpoints on AWS and Private Endpoints on Azure.

items.q: What four pieces of information does a Cloud Monitoring query in Grafana require, and how does that compare across all three clouds now covered?
items.a: Metric type, a label-based filter (narrowing to a specific resource/dimension), and an aggregation function over an alignment period -- functionally identical in purpose to CloudWatch's namespace+metric+dimensions+statistic and Azure Monitor's namespace+metric+resource+aggregation. All three clouds require the same four conceptual pieces -- which metric, filtered to what, aggregated how, over what time window -- just with different field names and syntax for expressing each one.

items.q: Why does Grafana's math expression feature do the Metric-Math-equivalent job on all three clouds rather than each cloud providing its own native version?
items.a: Only CloudWatch has a genuine server-side Metric Math feature; Azure Monitor and Cloud Monitoring have no native cross-metric-query math capability of their own. Grafana's own math expression layer (referencing queries by letter and combining them, e.g. $A / $B * 100) works identically regardless of which cloud's data source is feeding queries A and B, which is precisely why it's the more broadly useful skill to know well -- it's cloud-agnostic within Grafana even when the underlying platforms differ in their own native capabilities.

items.q: What is the fundamental philosophical difference between Cloud Composer and both Step Functions and Azure Data Factory?
items.a: Cloud Composer DAGs are defined as actual Python code files, not JSON state machine definitions or visual/JSON pipeline configurations. This means orchestration logic on Composer is written and version-controlled the same way application code is -- with real Python control flow, imports, and testing patterns available -- rather than being expressed in a more declarative, visually-oriented configuration format. It's a genuinely different orchestration philosophy, not just a syntax difference, and worth naming explicitly as the one clear differentiator in this otherwise-parallel section of the three clouds.

items.q: How does Airflow's dynamic task mapping (.expand()) achieve the same fan-out as a Step Functions Map state?
items.a: expand() takes a base task definition and a list of inputs, generating one task instance per input at DAG-run time, each running independently with its own retry and failure handling -- functionally identical to Map's per-item parallel branch behavior. The Python expression op_args=[[s] for s in SOURCE_LIST] generates one task per source in the list, achieving the same 50-parallel-independent-branches shape as the Step Functions and ADF versions of this exact pattern, just expressed as a Python list comprehension rather than a JSON ItemsPath reference.

items.q: When would you choose Cloud Workflows over Cloud Composer for a piece of orchestration?
items.a: Cloud Workflows suits simple, mostly-linear sequences of API calls -- lighter weight, YAML-defined, no persistent Airflow environment to manage or pay for. Cloud Composer is justified once you need genuine DAG complexity, Python-native task logic, a rich library of pre-built Operators for GCP services, or a scheduling/retry/monitoring feature set built for data pipeline orchestration specifically. The same heavier-orchestration-vs-lightweight-glue trade-off as Step Functions-vs-simple-Lambda or ADF-vs-Logic-Apps applies here.

items.q: Why is it inaccurate to describe BigQuery as simply 'Athena for GCP'?
items.a: Athena is fundamentally a query engine over externally-held files -- it has no native storage format of its own. BigQuery is a full data warehouse with its own optimized columnar storage, automatic query optimization, native streaming ingestion, and even built-in ML training via SQL -- querying external files in Cloud Storage is just one supported mode (via external tables) rather than BigQuery's primary operating model. The closer AWS analogy for BigQuery's native-storage mode is actually Redshift, with Athena only matching BigQuery's external-table mode specifically.

items.q: What are partitioning and clustering in BigQuery, and how do they combine to reduce query cost beyond what Athena's partition pruning alone achieves?
items.a: Partitioning (typically by date) prunes entire partitions from a scan based on a WHERE filter, the same mechanism as Athena. Clustering additionally sorts data within each partition by one or more frequently-filtered columns, letting BigQuery skip even more data within a matching partition when a clustered column is also filtered on. Athena has no direct clustering equivalent -- this two-layer optimization (partition prune, then cluster-based skip within the partition) is a genuine BigQuery-specific cost/performance capability.

items.q: How does BigQuery's flat-rate pricing model differ from Athena's pricing, and when would a team choose it?
items.a: On-demand pricing (pay per TB scanned) is the default and the direct equivalent of Athena's only pricing model. Flat-rate/capacity-based pricing lets an organization reserve dedicated query slots for a fixed cost regardless of query volume -- economically favorable for teams running consistently high query volume where per-TB-scanned costs would otherwise be unpredictable or higher in aggregate. Athena has no equivalent reserved-capacity option; this is a genuinely GCP-specific pricing lever.

items.q: How does Terraform remote state locking on GCP compare to the AWS S3+DynamoDB and Azure Blob-lease patterns?
items.a: GCS (Google Cloud Storage) as a Terraform backend uses Cloud Storage's native object generation/versioning mechanism to implement locking, without a separate lock table -- the same simplification pattern as Azure's Blob Storage lease-based locking, and a genuine reduction in setup complexity compared to needing a separate DynamoDB table alongside S3 on AWS.

items.q: What is the single strongest interview-ready statement to make about Terraform after seeing it applied across all three clouds in this plan?
items.a: That the actual Terraform discipline -- reading the plan output before every apply, using remote state for team safety, packaging repeated patterns as modules, and treating dashboards/alerts as code alongside infrastructure -- is completely cloud-agnostic. What changes between AWS, Azure, and GCP is only the provider block and the specific resource type names; the judgment and workflow around Terraform itself transfers without modification, which is precisely the kind of transferable-skill framing that distinguishes real experience from a AWS-only skillset with new vocabulary memorized on top.

items.q: What does VPC Service Controls protect against that a firewall rule or IAM policy alone doesn't, and why is there no precise 1:1 AWS/Azure equivalent?
items.a: VPC Service Controls creates a service perimeter that blocks data exfiltration even by an identity that IS otherwise authorized via IAM to access the resource, if that access attempt originates from outside the perimeter's trusted context (a different project, an unapproved network). This addresses a specific threat model -- a compromised or malicious authorized credential being used from an unexpected location -- that plain IAM policy and firewall rules don't cover on their own, since IAM only asks 'is this identity allowed,' not 'is this access attempt happening from a place we trust.' AWS and Azure have pieces of this idea spread across VPC endpoint policies and conditional access policies respectively, but no single service matches this specific perimeter-based exfiltration-prevention model as directly.

items.q: How do GCP Firewall Rules differ structurally from AWS Security Groups or Azure NSGs?
items.a: GCP Firewall Rules are defined once per VPC network and apply based on network tags or service accounts attached to instances, rather than being directly bound to a specific subnet (like an NSG often is) or a specific instance/ENI (like a Security Group is). This means the same firewall rule can apply consistently to any instance carrying a particular tag anywhere in the network, a more label-based and less topology-based model than the subnet- or instance-attachment patterns on AWS and Azure.

items.q: Walk through the full GCP-equivalent pipeline architecture end to end.
items.a: Cloud Composer's Airflow DAG triggers on a schedule, dynamically maps a fetch task across 50 sources in parallel, each landing data into a Cloud Storage raw zone. An ephemeral Dataproc cluster validates and transforms the data, writing either to a processed Cloud Storage zone or directly into partitioned, clustered BigQuery native tables. BigQuery serves as the queryable layer, with materialized pre-aggregated tables for anything queried repeatedly. Cloud Logging automatically captures every resource's logs with no manual routing step, log-based metrics and Alerting Policies cover the same conditions as the other two clouds, and Grafana on Cloud Monitoring + Cloud Logging provides the same unified dashboard experience.

items.q: After building the same pipeline conceptually on all three clouds, what is the single most valuable thing to say in an interview about this experience?
items.a: That the underlying architecture and judgment -- config-driven ingestion so adding a source is a data change not a code change, cost discipline through ephemeral compute and storage tiering, unified observability through Grafana regardless of the native monitoring service underneath, and Terraform's plan-review-apply discipline -- is genuinely cloud-agnostic. Naming the SPECIFIC structural differences explicitly (GCP's additive-only IAM, Azure's Resource Group cascading delete, BigQuery's native warehouse model versus Athena's file-query-only model) is what proves this is real transferable understanding, not a surface find-and-replace of AWS terminology.
